section_summary: This section completes a broad report on the first months of the Allied occupation, covering economic democratization, agrarian and labor reform, political parties, war-criminal arrests, shortages, public finance, and Japanese attitudes, followed by a calendar of events through November 20, 1945. It then contains diplomatic reporting on the Communist movement and electoral politics, a report from visiting American Christian leaders on conditions in Japan and Korea, and a despatch enclosing a Japanese magazine article demanding the removal of civilian and military leaders associated with prewar militarism. Recurring themes include responsibility for the war, the qualifications of future political candidates, democratization, economic distress, and the revival of Japanese Christianity.

subfiles.title: Continuation of report on occupation reforms, political parties, economic conditions, and public attitudes in Japan, with calendar of principal events
subfiles.about: A comprehensive assessment of political, social, and economic change during the first two and a half months of the Allied occupation of Japan.
subfiles.summary: The report describes the dissolution of the major zaibatsu, proposals for agrarian reform, new labor protections, administrative democratization, war-criminal arrests, and the formation and programs of Japan's postwar parties. It also surveys severe food, housing, production, unemployment, and financial problems and assesses Japanese reactions to surrender and occupation. The author concludes that initial occupation objectives had been achieved but that democratic habits remained weak and antidemocratic forces could revive. An appendix lists major occupation and Japanese political events from August 26 through November 20, 1945.

subfiles.title: Telegram 4016: Reestablishment of the Communist Youth League in Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; repeated to Chungking, Frankfurt, and Tokyo for Acting Political Adviser Atcheson
subfiles.about: Reports a TASS item claiming that the Communist Youth League had been reestablished in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The telegram relays a November 20 Tokyo TASS report that the Communist Youth League had been restored in Japan. It states that the Komsomol would guide democratic tendencies arising among Japanese youth.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 83: Political Parties in Japan—Developments During the Week Ending December 1, 1945
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a weekly report on Japanese political parties and renews a recommendation for rules governing eligibility in the coming elections.
subfiles.summary: Despatch transmitting a report on party developments for the week ending December 1, recommending action on the November 24 proposal to bar unsuitable candidates.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to the Supreme Commander: Japanese Political Parties, Week Ending December 1, 1945
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Acting U.S. Political Adviser
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Urges the occupation authorities to define electoral qualifications and describes lists being prepared to identify Diet members associated with wartime political bodies.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson reports the mission is classifying House members by their ties to wartime nationalist groups and argues a SCAP directive restricting implicated candidates would aid democracy.

subfiles.title: Political Developments During the Week to December 1, 1945
subfiles.from: John K. Emmerson, Foreign Service Officer
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, through the Acting U.S. Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Analyzes the Diet parties, the war-responsibility debate, Communist organization, and cooperation among minor right-wing parties.
subfiles.summary: Emmerson reports that the main parties lack democratic coherence, the House adopted a weak war-responsibility resolution, and the Diet is unlikely to purge itself without a SCAP directive.

subfiles.title: Memorandum forwarding a report on Japan
subfiles.to: John Carter Vincent, Director, Office of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Forwards a voluntary report by four religious leaders recently returned from Japan and Korea.
subfiles.summary: Carroll forwards observations on Japan and Korea given voluntarily at a YMCA conference, not through interrogation, as useful background on conditions and public attitudes.

subfiles.title: Report on Japan by Four Religious Leaders
subfiles.from: Douglas Horton, Walter W. Van Kirk, Bishop James C. Baker, and Dr. Schaefer; notes by Frank B. Lenz
subfiles.about: Records the observations of four American Christian leaders after a twenty-three-day visit to occupied Japan, with a shorter account of conditions in Korea.
subfiles.summary: The speakers describe political division and institutional deterioration in Korea, followed by the warm reception given them by Japanese Christians and the friendly relations between occupation troops and civilians. They report that Japanese churches and Christian schools survived wartime repression but suffered extensive physical destruction, shortages, and homelessness. Particular attention is given to Toyohiko Kagawa, Michi Kawai, women's political participation, the Emperor's interest in Christianity, and MacArthur's occupation policies. The delegation calls for missionaries, teachers, Bibles, hymnals, Christian literature, food, clothing, and a church relief program.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 86: Translation of Magazine Article Entitled “Public Men Who Danced to the Tune of the Militarists”
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Acting United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Encloses a Shinsei article arguing that civilian politicians and bureaucrats who supported militarism must be removed from public life.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson summarizes an article blaming militarists, elder statesmen, Diet members and bureaucrats for the road to war, regarding its general treatment as sound and as evidence of support for a thorough purge.

subfiles.title: “Public Men Who Danced to the Tune of the Militarists”
subfiles.to: Shinsei readers; translated for the U.S. Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Argues that Japan cannot be democratized without purging the civilian and military ruling groups responsible for the rise of militarism.
subfiles.summary: The article says the Higashikuni and Shidehara governments preserved compromised elites, traces the rise of army power, and accuses politicians and officials of failing to resist the army and aiding the Tōjō regime.
